questions.question_text:
A council wants to determine public opinion on building a new skate park.
They interview $200$ people entering a youth recreation centre on a Saturday afternoon.
Why is this sample unrepresentative of the whole municipality?

options.text: It uses convenience sampling at a single venue, heavily over-representing young active residents
The sample size of $200$ is too small for any municipal survey
options.why: The number 200 alone does not show whether a sample is adequate. The stated defect is selection at one venue rather than fair coverage of the municipality.

options.text: It relies on a stratified random design across suburbs
options.why: The method described is location-based convenience sampling, not stratified random sampling.

options.text: It violates ethical privacy rules by asking about recreational activities
options.why: The stem describes a biased selection location; asking about a skate park does not itself establish a privacy breach.

questions.solution_text:
People who do not attend this youth recreation centre at that time cannot be selected, and attendees may have different views from other residents.
It uses convenience sampling at a single venue, heavily over-representing young active residents.

questions.question_text:
A news website posts an online poll asking: 'Should Sunday trading hours be extended?' $5000$ readers vote.
Why cannot this sample be used to conclude what the general population thinks?

options.text: It is a self-selected sample covering only website visitors who chose to vote
The sample size of $5000$ is mathematically insufficient
options.why: The number 5000 does not correct the restricted coverage or self-selection. No rule about a minimum sample size is given.

options.text: The survey question is double-barrelled
options.why: The question asks a single simple question about Sunday trading hours.

options.text: The survey violates respondent anonymity
options.why: The stem does not say whether individuals can be identified. The stated problem is who could vote and who chose to respond.

questions.solution_text:
Only website visitors who choose to vote are included. Their views may differ from visitors who do not vote and from the wider population.
It is a self-selected sample covering only website visitors who chose to vote.

questions.question_text:
A national airline with $10\,000\,000$ annual passengers surveys $4$ passengers selected at random to evaluate passenger satisfaction.
Why is this a poor basis for representing passenger satisfaction?

options.text: The very small sample may miss much of the variety of passenger experiences
Random selection always produces biased results
options.why: Random selection does not systematically favour particular members. With just four passengers, however, the result may vary greatly by chance.

options.text: The airline used an unstratified quota system
options.why: The stem states passengers were selected at random, not via an unstratified quota system.

options.text: The survey questions must have been leading
options.why: The flaw is the tiny sample size, not the wording of the questions.

questions.solution_text:
Changing one of four replies changes the sample percentage by $\frac14\times100\%=25\%$. Four passengers may miss much of the range of experiences.
The very small sample may miss much of the variety of passenger experiences.

questions.question_text:
A primary school has $300$ boys and $200$ girls (total $500$ students).
A researcher selects a sample of $30$ boys and $20$ girls.
Is this sample representative regarding student gender?

options.text: Yes, because boys make up $60\%$ and girls make up $40\%$ of both the population and the sample
No, because a representative sample must contain equal numbers of boys and girls ($25$ each)
options.why: Equal numbers would misrepresent the population, which is 60% boys and 40% girls.

options.text: No, because stratified sampling cannot be used for gender
options.why: Gender is a standard, valid demographic variable for stratified sampling.

options.text: No, because the total sample of $50$ is too small for a school of $500$
options.why: The question asks about gender proportions: 30 of 50 are boys and 20 are girls, matching 60% and 40%. Sample size alone does not change that comparison.

questions.solution_text:
Boys: $\frac{300}{500}=60\%$ in population and $\frac{30}{50}=60\%$ in sample. Girls: $\frac{200}{500}=40\%$ in population and $\frac{20}{50}=40\%$ in sample.
Yes, because boys make up $60\%$ and girls make up $40\%$ of both the population and the sample.

questions.question_text: A company has $2000$ employees in four departments of different sizes. Which design gives every employee a fair chance of being selected from the whole company?

options.text: Generating $100$ unique random numbers linked to employee IDs from the complete staff registry
Interviewing the first $100$ employees who arrive at the head office on Monday morning
options.why: This is convenience sampling that excludes remote workers, shift workers, and late arrivals.

options.text: Placing a suggestion box in the staff cafeteria for one week
options.why: This is voluntary response: only people who choose to use the cafeteria suggestion box are included. Their views may differ from those of other employees.

options.text: Selecting $25$ employees from each of the $4$ departments regardless of department size
options.why: Sampling equal counts across departments of unequal size distorts proportional representation.

questions.solution_text:
Choosing 100 different employee IDs at random from the complete registry gives each employee an equal chance of selection. The other methods restrict coverage, rely on volunteers or give unequal selection chances across differently sized departments.
Generating $100$ unique random numbers linked to employee IDs from the complete staff registry.

questions.question_text:
A company employs $1200$ factory workers and $300$ office workers (total $1500$).
A survey selects $50$ factory workers and $50$ office workers.
Why is this sample unrepresentative?

options.text: Office workers make up $20\%$ of the workforce but $50\%$ of the sample, so they are heavily over-represented
Factory workers are over-represented in the sample
options.why: Factory workers make up 80% of staff but only 50% of the sample, so they are under-represented.

options.text: The sample is representative because both workplace groups have equal voice
options.why: Representative sampling requires proportions matching the population, not equal arbitrary counts.

options.text: The sample size of $100$ is too small for $1500$ employees
options.why: Regardless of whether 100 responses are enough for the wider purpose, the stated sample has the wrong group shares: 50% office workers rather than 20%.

questions.solution_text:
Factory workers make up $\frac{1200}{1500}=80\%$ of the population but only $\frac{50}{100}=50\%$ of the sample. Office workers are over-represented at $50\%$ instead of $20\%$.
Office workers make up $20\%$ of the workforce but $50\%$ of the sample, so they are heavily over-represented.

questions.question_text:
A telecommunications company surveys customer satisfaction by randomly generating landline telephone numbers.
Why does this method produce an unrepresentative sample of all mobile phone users?

options.text: It excludes mobile-only households, whose views may differ from those of landline users
Landline numbers cannot be selected randomly by computers
options.why: Computers can generate landline numbers at random, but doing so still excludes mobile-only households.

options.text: The sample size of landline calls is always too small
options.why: The issue is undercoverage in the sampling frame, not the quantity of calls made.

options.text: Telecommunications surveys violate commercial privacy regulations
options.why: No information about consent or handling personal data is given. The stated problem is that mobile-only users cannot be selected.

questions.solution_text:
Random landline calls cannot reach mobile-only households. Their views may differ from those of mobile users who also have a landline.
It excludes mobile-only households, whose views may differ from those of landline users.

questions.question_text:
A state transport department wants a sample of its daily rail commuters who use smartcards.
It has a complete list of these $100\,000$ commuters, groups the list by travel zone in proportion to the numbers of commuters in each zone, and randomly selects $1000$ commuters with email and SMS reminders.
Which features help this design represent the stated population?

options.text: It uses the complete target-population list, matches travel-zone proportions, and encourages selected commuters to respond
It allows commuters to opt into the survey voluntarily on social media
options.why: The method uses the ticketing database and targeted contact, not open social media opt-in.

options.text: It guarantees that every commuter gives positive feedback on rail services
options.why: A fair sampling design helps represent the population; it does not guarantee matching views or positive feedback.

options.text: It surveys an equal number of passengers from every station regardless of passenger volume
options.why: The design matches travel-zone shares of commuters; it does not select equal numbers from every station regardless of the number of commuters.

questions.solution_text:
The list covers the stated smartcard-using daily commuters, and the selections match their travel-zone shares. Reminders encourage selected commuters to respond.
Check who actually replies before drawing a conclusion; the design does not guarantee perfect representation or include commuters outside the stated population.
It uses the complete target-population list, matches travel-zone proportions, and encourages selected commuters to respond.
